title: The Heron Warehouse
summary: Night at the wharves: the King's grain re-sacked under a heron, a barge that sails on the ebb, and the true book that can hang a gentleman.
assumes: Tonight's loading at the Heron is still going on: the barge hasn't sailed or been stopped, and the true book is still in the Heron.

Master Sallow is still free (not arrested, not fled the city) and still coming to the Heron at the midnight bell. (The player suspecting him, or even naming him to the watch, doesn't change that: only his arrest or flight does.)
background: This is the same night as the Drowned Rat and the morning at the granary where Wendell Prout was found hanged. What happened in them is in what happened just before this scene, and that wins: where Hobb is, whether Sallow has been warned, what the player carries (Prout's page, Hobb's token) and how they stand with Kell. If nothing happened before: the player knows Hobb works nights at the Heron for a gentleman, Hobb is at work on the hoist, and Sallow hasn't been warned.

cast.name: Hepzibah Grist
cast.group: Hep Grist and her re-sacking gang, six porters in grain-white with knives and sack-needles

cast.name: Big Hobb Mallory
cast.called: the big porter with the bandaged hand

cast.name: Master Josiah Sallow
cast.called: the gentleman with the silver-topped cane
cast.group: Master Sallow, his lantern-boy and the Crake brothers, two hired river-bruisers

members.name: the talking Crake
members.look: An enormous river-bruiser in a reefer jacket, with a cudgel and a great deal to say about it.

members.name: the silent Crake
members.look: His identical brother, who has never been heard to say anything at all.

members.name: the lantern-boy
members.look: A yawning boy of ten with a lantern on a pole, who would very much like to be somewhere else.

facts.in-as-a-hand: The player is in at the Heron as one of Hep's hands, taken on at the river door with a sack in their arms: to the gang they're crew, and working the floor with their head down (carrying, slitting, sewing, fetching) needs no roll. Only going where a hand wouldn't (up the counting-box stair, a hand on the book, the Master's elbow) gets them looked at.
facts.master-here: Master Sallow has come to the Heron.
facts.book-in-hand: The player has the true book in their hands.
facts.book-seen: The player has seen inside the true book: the 'lost' wagons by their Granary Roll numbers, with Sallow's initials on every page.
facts.book-gone: The true book has been destroyed: burned, or gone into the river.
facts.heron-ablaze: Fire has taken hold of the Heron.
facts.barge-sunk: The barge Patience has gone down with the King's grain in her.

routes.when: The player is inside the Heron, unnoticed or taken for someone who belongs there (in at the river door with Hobb's token or his help, past Saul, as a hand in Hep's gang, or any other way established in play).

The player tries to slip into the Heron unseen: past Saul's deaf side and the sleeping dog, or along the plank walk and in at the river door while the gang's backs are turned. (Walking in with a sack on their shoulder, as one of the gang, isn't slipping in unseen: that's going in to work, with no dice.)

check.reason: to slip into the Heron unseen
check.success: They're in, in the shadow of the wheat-ear stacks, with the whole floor in front of them and nobody the wiser.
check.failure: Something gives them away (a plank that creaks, a dog that wasn't asleep, a porter who looks round at the wrong moment) and the alarm goes up. They're not caught yet, but the wharf is looking for them.

routes.when: The player shows a brass heron token (Hobb's, or one like it) at the river door's grille to be let in, with or without a story to go with it. No dice: the token is what the gang show, so whoever's nearest inside draws the bolt, looks them over ('You're not Hobb'), and pushes a sack into their arms, because Hep is short of hands: they're in as one of her hands, and working the floor needs no roll. A story told with the token isn't a bluff to roll for.

The player goes in to work, token or none: shoulders a sack (one waiting on the plank walk, a split one off the hoist) and walks in at the river door with the gang as if they belong, or answers Hep's shout for hands at the river door, or asks there to be taken on for the night, or knocks at the grille for Hobb if he agreed at the Rat to let them in. No dice: Hep is short-handed on the Assembly eve (half the river's drunk) and anyone with a sack on their shoulder is crew until proven otherwise, so she puts them to work and asks who they are afterwards, if ever: they're in as one of her hands, and working the floor needs no roll. A story told with it isn't a bluff to roll for.

With no heron token to show, the player tries to bluff their way in past Saul or whoever answers the river door with a story that isn't true: the Saltmere factor's man, someone sent by the Master, a hand that somebody sent for when nobody did. (Showing Hobb's token at the grille, and going in to work with a sack on their shoulder or at Hep's shout for hands, are ways in of their own with no dice, whatever story goes with them: they aren't this.)

check.reason: to talk your way into the Heron
check.success: Whoever's at the door believes it and stands aside. They're in, and expected to behave like whoever they said they were.
check.failure: It doesn't wash. The door stays shut, and whoever was at it is now watching the wharf for them; the next way in will have to be a different one.

routes.when: The player tries to make friends with Duchess before she raises the wharf: food, patience, a way with dogs.

check.reason: to win Duchess over before she raises the wharf
check.success: Duchess decides they're the best thing that's happened to her all night and leans her whole weight on them. Saul, who trusts her nose over his own eyes, unbends: anyone she likes can't be all bad, and all's well.
check.failure: Duchess takes the offering, and very nearly the hand with it, and sets up a baying fit to wake the river. Saul is on his feet with the lantern, staring hard into the dark.

routes.when: The player tries to get in from the river side the hard way: along the piles under the floor, up the hoist rope, or across the barge and in through the loading door.

check.reason: to climb into the Heron from the river side
check.success: Cold, wet to the knees and very quiet, they come up through the river door in the shadow of the chute, and nobody looks round.
check.failure: A pile is slimed with weed, or the hoist swings: they go into the river to the chest, and the cold drives the breath out of them. They're clinging to a pile under the floor, unseen for now, with Duchess barking somewhere overhead.

routes.when: The player has been out on the wharf a long while (at least six exchanges at this point) without getting in, or is waiting to see who comes: the midnight bell, a smell of lavender along the wharf, and the Master arrives at the land door.
The player has the true book in their hands: lifted, taken, snatched or handed over by Scrope.
The player has had a good look inside the true book, or had it read to them: the 'lost' wagons by their Granary Roll numbers, with the Master's initials on every page.
The player tries to lift the true book from under Scrope's hand without him or the gang seeing.

check.reason: to lift the ledger from under the clerk's hand
check.success: Scrope turns to trim the lamp, and when he turns back his hand comes down on bare desk. The book is under the player's coat.
check.failure: Scrope's hand clamps down on the book with a squeak like a trodden mouse, and heads turn all over the floor.

routes.when: The player tries to persuade Scrope to give them the true book or to swear to it (for Prout's sake, for his own neck, for the King), where his terror of the Master could still win. (Proof that puts it beyond doubt for him needs no dice.)

check.reason: to persuade the clerk to give up his ledger
check.success: Scrope looks at the book for a long time, then closes it, does up the clasp and holds it out in both hands. 'It balances,' he says. 'Every page. Wendell would want it to balance.'
check.failure: Scrope hugs the book to his chest and shakes his head, white as paper: not with the Master coming. He hasn't called for anyone. Yet.

routes.when: Challenged on the floor (by Hep, the gang or Scrope), the player tries to bluff that they belong here.

check.reason: to bluff your way through a challenge on the floor
check.success: Whoever challenged them grunts, satisfied, and goes back to work.
check.failure: Nobody believes a word. Hep shouts for hands, and the gang put their sacks down.

routes.when: The player has been caught out on the floor and is being held (by Hep's gang, Saul or Hobb) to wait for the Master.
The player attacks Sallow, the Crakes or Hep's gang, meaning to hurt them now: a real fight, not a shove to get past someone.

The player has been inside a good while (at least five exchanges at this point), or has said they're waiting for the Master himself (hiding to see who comes in at the bell, with nothing else in hand): the midnight bell, lavender on the air, and the Master comes in at the land door. A player carrying sacks and keeping their head down while they wait for a word with Hobb, a look at the book or a chance at it isn't waiting for the Master: they're working the floor, and the floor gets its exchanges.

Sallow has been caught at the loading of the King's grain before witnesses who will swear to it (Kell, Hep's gang, Scrope, Hobb or the player), Kell has arrested him, and he is actually held: he has given himself up (the cane handed over, his hands up) or been beaten or overpowered, and his Crakes have stood down or been dealt with. The words of arrest alone, with Sallow defiant and his Crakes still beside him, aren't this: that is the moment he draws.
The player has the true book in their hands: lifted, taken, snatched or handed over by Scrope.
The player has had a good look inside the true book, or had it read to them: the 'lost' wagons by their Granary Roll numbers, with the Master's initials on every page.
The true book has been destroyed: thrown in the brazier and burned, or gone into the river.
The player tries to fool Sallow to his face: passing as the Saltmere factor's agent, a buyer, someone sent from the palace, or one of the gang.

check.success: Sallow believes it, for now, and treats them as what they claimed to be: he may even initial the page in front of them, or hand them the book to admire.
check.failure: Sallow smiles thinly: he knows a liar, having been one professionally for years. 'Crake,' he says, and both of them move.

routes.when: The player confronts Sallow in front of his own people to break his nerve: naming the murder, the grain, the proof, the gallows.

check.reason: to break Sallow's nerve in front of his own people
check.success: The courtesy cracks. Sallow goes the colour of tallow and offers money too fast, and his own people see it: the gang stop working, and the Crakes look at each other.
check.failure: Sallow hears them out with polite boredom, then says, 'Regrettably, the wharves are dangerous at night,' and the Crakes start forward.

routes.when: The player tries to turn Hep and her gang, Scrope or Hobb against the Master in front of him, so that they'll swear to what they've seen.

check.reason: to turn the Master's own people against him
check.success: Hep looks at her gang, then at the Master, and puts down her knife. 'We'll swear,' she says. 'All of us. For them.' One by one, the gang stand behind her.
check.failure: Nobody moves: for now they're more frightened of him than of the gallows. Sallow smiles.

routes.when: The player makes a grab for the true book while Sallow or the Crakes have it, or as it goes towards the brazier, the river or the barge.

check.reason: to snatch the true book before it's lost
check.success: They have it, singed or wet but whole, and everyone in the Heron is looking at them.
check.failure: Sallow is quicker than he looks: the book goes into the brazier, over the side or down the chute, and it's going fast.

routes.when: The player has been overpowered and thrown in the river, or shut up somewhere in the Heron, by the Crakes or the gang, and nobody has got them out.
Sallow, exposed with proof in front of witnesses he can't buy, has drawn the sword from his cane and set the Crakes on the player: blades are out and the fight has started.
The player attacks Sallow, the Crakes or Hep's gang, meaning to hurt them now: a real fight, not a shove to get past someone.

The Master has been here a good while (at least six exchanges at this point), or the player is hiding or dithering with nothing in hand and nothing they're waiting for: the second bell, the last sacks go down, and the barge casts off on the ebb with the King's grain aboard. A player waiting for a moment they've named (the Master at the book to initial the page, a chance at the book, the moment to signal Kell) isn't dithering: that moment comes first.

anytime.when: The player leaves the Heron with the true book in their hands (out of a door, off the wharf, or over the side into the dark) and nobody is holding them.
Fire has taken hold of the Heron: a naked light in the grain dust, a brazier knocked over, a diversion got out of hand.
The barge is going down with the King's grain in her: holed, swamped, or cut loose and swept onto the piers.
The player gives up and leaves the wharf without the proof, leaving the Heron to its night's work.

caught.title: The wharves are dangerous at night

way-in.what: There's a way into the Heron without a key: the river door opens to anyone who shows a brass heron token at its grille; Saul at the land door is deaf on his left side and takes to whoever Duchess takes to; and Hep's gang is short-handed and puts anyone carrying a sack to work.
placedWith: Saul and Duchess at the land door
Hep shouting for hands at the river door

kings-grain.what: The Heron's grain is the King's: the gang are slitting sacks stamped with the palace wheat-ear and pouring them into heron sacks, and the empties are waiting to go in the river weighted with stones.
placedWith: the heap of empty wheat-ear sacks
a sack split on the hoist
kings-grain.unlocks: proof in plain sight, and witnesses who've handled it

true-book.what: Mister Scrope's true book, up in the counting-box, records every 'lost' wagon by its Granary Roll number with Sallow's initials on every page, and the Master comes at the midnight bell to initial tonight's.
placedWith: Hep, who wants the count right before the Master comes
Saul, who must have the land door open for the Master at the bell
true-book.unlocks: the proof, and the moment to catch Sallow in the act
